results.content:
## Questions

### Is Statefold a coding agent?−

No. Statefold runs the native harnesses you choose (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi and Gemini CLI) and gives them a sandbox, git access and a thread that persists. The agent is still the agent you know.

### Will it ask me to approve every command?+

No. Every thread runs with full access inside its own isolated sandbox, so commands and edits never wait on you. Agents are told to make reasonable, reversible decisions and only ask when they genuinely can’t proceed. They ask before force-pushing or merging.

### Can I use my own accounts?+

Yes. Connect your own harness subscriptions and API keys. They stay outside the container and are swapped in at egress, and you can see health and quota per connection. [...] ### What does Statefold remember?+

With memory on for a project, threads save durable notes after completed turns: conventions, decisions and your feedback. New threads recall what’s relevant on any harness. Personal preferences stay private, and you can inspect, edit or forget any note.

### Do I have to push my local work first?+

No. The CLI hands off your current checkout, including uncommitted work, without touching your local branch.

statefold [...] ### How do I know when a thread is done?+

Status is derived from what’s running and linked: Working, Needs you, Ready to review, Done, Failed or Limited. A thread is Done when its pull request merges. You get one notification when it goes idle while you’re away and one when it needs you.

### How do agents on different harnesses work together?+

By delegation. A thread can start child threads on any harness or model, wait for their results and continue. You can also fork a thread from any finished turn, or attach another thread as context with @.

results.title: GitHub - ioteverythin/statefold: Framework-agnostic, event-sourced state platform for AI agents (LangGraph, CrewAI, Agno, MCP) · GitHub
results.content:
A framework-agnostic, event-sourced state platform for AI agents — works under LangGraph, CrewAI, Agno, raw tools, or MCP.

statefold landing page

The observability console: KPI bar, per-session cost/error table, and a run waterfall with a time-travel slider — replay any run step by step and watch state and spend rewind.

statefold console — run waterfall with time-travel

State is a fold over an append-only event log, not a mutable blob. That one choice gives you durable resume, time-travel, replay, and cheap branching for free — the things that turn "a memory library" into a platform. [...] `from statefold.adapters.generic import SessionState s = SessionState(store, tenant="acme", agent="bot", session="sess-1") await s.add_message("user", "book a hotel") await s.set(stage="searching") await s.remember("user prefers window seats")`

Because every adapter writes to the same store, state is shared across frameworks: a memory saved by an Agno agent is recallable by a CrewAI crew or a raw MCP agent on the same scope.

Any MCP-capable agent (raw, CrewAI, Agno, a Claude/GPT tool loop) gets durable state by adding one server — no framework integration:

`pip install -e ".[mcp]" statefold-mcp # in-memory (ephemeral) STATEFOLD_DSN=postgresql://localhost/statefold statefold-mcp # durable` [...] statefold models the four memory types agents actually need, on two scopes:

| Type | What it holds | How |
---
| Working | current messages + state bag | the folded state itself — `session.working_memory()` |
| Semantic | facts, preferences | `remember(text)` (default kind) |
| Episodic | past experiences with provenance | `end_episode(summary, outcome=...)` / `recall_episodes(query)` |
| Procedural | learned how-tos | `learn_procedure(text)` |

Levels: `level="session"` dies with the session; `level="agent"` is true long-term memory, shared across every session of that agent. Episodic and procedural memories are agent-level by default — that's the point:

results.title: Top Devin AI alternatives for autonomous coding in 2026 | Blog — Northflank
results.content:
Choose Factory if you want autonomous software engineering workflows covering coding, reviews, and other development tasks. Choose Amp if you want a flexible coding agent that can run locally or remotely and continue working while you're disconnected. Choose Cursor Cloud Agents if your team already uses Cursor, OpenHands if you want an open-source agent you can self-host, or Replit Agent if you want to build and deploy applications from prompts.

Choose Northflank if you want to run the coding agents you prefer on infrastructure you control, with isolated, persistent environments, self-serve BYOC, GPU workloads for self-hosted models, and the application infrastructure needed to test and deploy what agents build. [...] Amp is an AI coding agent that works through the terminal and web, allowing developers to delegate coding tasks locally or remotely. Its Orbs feature provides cloud environments where agents can continue working after the developer disconnects, with the ability to monitor and manage tasks from other devices. Amp supports multiple model providers and flexible authentication options, making it suitable for both interactive development and unattended coding workflows.

Best for: Developers and teams that want flexible coding agents with remote execution, multi-model support, and the ability to manage tasks across devices.

Pricing: Free Hobby tier, paid plans starting at $20/month, and custom Enterprise options. [...] Cursor Cloud Agents run coding tasks in remote cloud environments rather than on your local machine. They can edit code, run commands, and test changes, making them useful for developers who want to delegate longer tasks while continuing to use Cursor as their main editor. Cursor also offers options for running agent tool execution on self-hosted machines.

Best for: teams already using Cursor that want to delegate coding tasks to remote agents without changing their editor workflow.

Pricing: requires an eligible Cursor plan, with agent usage charged according to the applicable plan and model pricing.
